Comparison with other software

Source: vignettes/articles/software-comparison.Rmd
software-comparison.Rmd

A coeluting compound contributes several ion traces with the same elution profile. A single chromatogram already contains that information. Across a batch, repeated spectra add evidence, while retention time, concentration and peak shape can vary. The workflows below use different parts of this information to separate components.

Workflow How components are resolved and counted Background and noise How samples are used Access and source
GCMSprime A peak-shape dictionary supplies candidate peaks. A penalized likelihood selects rank with nonnegative spectra and log-concave profiles. The model fits a smooth baseline and estimates quasi-Poisson overdispersion by default. Fits one sample directly or shares spectra across a batch, with disk-backed refinement. Mathematical basis Free, GPL open source. Repository
GNPS/MSHub Within each aligned retention-time group, NMF separates the matrix of peak integrals. Increases in explained sum of squares guide the component count. Noise filtering and baseline correction precede factorization. Uses multiple samples for deconvolution. GNPS can also use externally deconvoluted spectra for networking. Aksenov et al. (2021) Free hosted workflow with a GNPS account. Public code under the repository’s nonprofit-use licence. Source · Licence
PARADISe Fits candidate PARAFAC2 models within retention intervals. The published workflow includes reviewing the intervals and component counts. Baseline and tail contributions can enter as factors in the least-squares model. Fits multiple chromatograms with a common spectral mode and the PARAFAC2 cross-product constraint. Johnsen et al. (2017) · Protocol Free Community and paid Professional editions, distributed as applications. Kromath
mzmine / ADAP-GC Detected ion peaks define local windows. ADAP-GC 4.0 uses clustering-assisted multivariate curve resolution. Peak detection and the selected module define preprocessing and separation. Deconvolves individual chromatograms before batch feature alignment. Smirnov et al. (2019) · mzmine guide Free mzmine Community licence for eligible academic users. Commercial use requires a paid plan. MIT-licensed public source · Plans
MS-DIAL Uses model peaks to extract EI spectra from detected peaks. Smoothing, peak detection and deconvolution settings guide local extraction. Extracts spectra per chromatogram, then aligns features across files. Lai et al. (2018) Free download and LGPL-3 source. Vendor readers can have separate terms. MsdialWorkbench
XCMS + CAMERA XCMS detects features. CAMERA uses retention time, peak shape and cross-sample evidence to build pseudospectra. Upstream peak detection and integration supply the feature list. Originally developed for LC–MS annotation. Groups detected features across samples. Kuhl et al. (2012) Free, GPL open source. XCMS · CAMERA
eRah Local covariance and orthogonal signal deconvolution separate coeluting signals. Noise filtering and baseline removal precede deconvolution. Deconvolves individual chromatograms, then aligns spectra and can recover missing entries. Domingo-Almenara et al. (2016) Free, GPL open source. CRAN
AMDIS Component perception identifies candidates. Selected ion chromatograms supply model shapes for spectrum extraction. Local noise and background estimates guide component perception and extraction. Deconvolves individual chromatograms and supports batch processing. Stein (1999) Free standalone binary. NIST distributes the application without public source. NIST download

What MSHub deconvolves

The GNPS implementation first groups aligned peaks by retention time. For each group it forms a samples-by-ions matrix of peak integrals. Its NMF gives a sample abundance and a mass spectrum for each component in the group. The rank search compares successive improvements in explained sum of squares. With no scan axis in its input, the factorization cannot estimate a time-resolved elution profile for each component in each sample or require its ions to follow one common profile. The NMF therefore has no component profile on which to impose unimodality. MSHub implementation

MSHub chooses rank automatically using fixed rules in the code. It rounds the percentage of explained sum of squares, stops when adding a component improves it by fewer than five percentage points, and has an additional stopping rule for two consecutive equal improvements. In GCMSprime the rank score uses a penalty on the number of components and occurrences, evaluated with the selected noise model. MSHub rank search · GCMSprime rank criterion

The matrix has rank at most one for a single sample. Even with multiple samples, two coeluting compounds with a fixed abundance ratio contribute a rank-one matrix. If their sample abundance vectors are a and ca and their spectra are s_1 and s_2, their summed contribution is a(s_1 + c s_2)^\mathsf{T}. Distinct profiles across scans can supply separation evidence within a single run. GCMSprime retains this scan-level information in the fit.

The public MSHub code switches to maximum-based spectrum extraction below five samples. The GNPS guide recommends another deconvolution workflow below about ten files. Networking and library search can then use the spectra produced by that external tool. MSHub sample-count check · GNPS guide

What the coupled model changes

For each component in each sample, GCMSprime multiplies a single elution profile by its shared mass spectrum. Every ion contributed by the component therefore follows the same profile in that sample. The profiles may change width, shift or tail across samples. Coupling enters the fit through the shared spectrum, and the rank penalty counts that spectrum once, with a separate amplitude for each occurrence. The objective and constraints are given in the algorithm article.

PARAFAC uses a common profile for each component up to amplitude. PARAFAC2 allows different profiles but constrains their cross-products to be constant across samples after separating the sample amplitudes. If a broadening acid peak changes its normalized overlap with a neighbouring compound, that constant cross-product assumption restricts the fit. GCMSprime allows the overlap to vary while requiring each profile to be log-concave. The beer example shows a broad, asymmetric acid peak in a single run.

With count noise, fitting the baseline together with the peaks lets the model use the original intensity and its mean-dependent variance. A background-subtracted trace is useful for display. The count model itself uses the sum of background and peak contributions.

For measured runtime, compound recovery and memory layout, see the 16-sample simulation and full-beer application.
